unesco.title: Morna, musical practice of Cabo Verde
unesco.description: Morna, musical practice of Cabo Verde is a traditional Cape Verdean musical and choreographic practice with instrumental accompaniment that incorporates voice, music, poetry, and dance. Morna can be either sung or played only with instruments, mainly chordophones, including the guitar, violin, ten-string guitar, replaced with a cavaquinho in the twentieth century, and the ukulele. Several other instruments have now been introduced – such as the piano, percussion and bass – but the guitar remains the preferred instrument. The lyric poetry can be improvised, with topics including love, departure, separation, reunion, longing, the ocean and the motherland. While in the past the lyrics were also composed in Portuguese, nowadays it is mainly composed in Cape Verdean Creole. Bearers and practitioners of the element include instrument players, singers, poets, and composers, who perform, disseminate and transmit the practice to the younger generations. Currently, some bearers are also opening teaching centres, and as a genre Morna is also practised by formal groups. Morna is a fundamental aspect of Cape Verdean social and cultural life, as it performed at key life events, such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions. Transmission has been carried out by the community, through workshops, radio programmes, performances, festivals, and the musical contest entitled ‘Todo Mundo Canta’, which takes place on every island.

profile.name: morna
profile.tagline: Cape Verde's national ballroom dance of slow sorrow, romance, and ocean longing.
profile.insight: In a Cape Verdean morna, a couple sways together twice to one side per bar, mirroring the melancholic pull of the ocean and the painful departure for foreign shores.
profile.profile: The morna is the national music and ballroom dance of Cape Verde, characterized by a slow tempo, binary meter, and themes of saudade, love, and separation. Performed in pairs with a gentle embracing arm and hand-hold, dancers execute two synchronized body swings to one side per bar, shifting to the opposite side on the next. The genre blends acoustic instrumentation like the guitar, violin, and cavaquinho, and was proclaimed an UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2019.
profile.profile_long: The morna is a traditional musical and choreographic practice originating from the islands of Cape Verde, widely regarded as the nation's profound cultural symbol. Historically rooted in the 18th century on Boa Vista Island—with some scholars linking its early rhythms to the lundum and local working songs called choros—the morna matured into a distinct artistic tradition by the 19th century. Initially a simpler genre often featuring satire or social commentary with a quicker tempo, it underwent a profound transformation in the early 20th century through poet and composer Eugénio Tavares on Brava Island, who infused it with deep romanticism, lyricism, and themes of love, departure, and saudade. Later, in the 1930s and 1940s, composer B. Leza introduced passing chords known as the 'meio-tom brasileiro' in São Vicente, enriching the traditional cycle-of-fifths harmonic structure. As a dance, the morna is an intimate ballroom genre performed in pairs. Dancers embrace their partner with one arm while holding hands with the other, executing a precise choreography of two body swings to one side during a musical bar, followed by two swings to the other side in the subsequent bar. Musically, it is defined by a lento tempo, binary meter, syncopated melodies, and acoustic chordophones such as the guitar (*violão*), ten-string guitar (*viola*), cavaquinho, and violin (*rabeca*). International recognition soared through iconic interpreters like Cesária Évora, culminating in its inscription as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2019.

sections.origins_and_history: The oral tradition places the origins of the morna on Boa Vista Island in the 18th century, potentially evolving from a cross between local working choros and the introduced lundum. By the 19th century, it was a fully formed genre, with compositions like 'Brada Maria' documented around 1870. The 2nd period, led by Eugénio Tavares in the early 20th century on Brava Island, introduced slower tempos and romantic lyricism focused on love and separation. The 3rd period in the 1930s and 1940s saw São Vicente composer B. Leza incorporate Brazilian-influenced passing chords, expanding harmonic possibilities beyond the traditional cycle of fifths. The 4th period (1950s-1970s) coincided with the rise of the coladeira and the incorporation of political and homeland themes. Recent years have seen increased artistic freedom, with contemporary composers experimenting with chord sequences and fusions.
sections.how_it_is_danced: As a dance the morna is a ballroom dance, danced in pairs. The performers dance with an arm embracing the partner, while with the other arm they hold hands. The dancing is made through two body swings to one side in a music's bar, while in the next bar the swinging is to the other side.
sections.music_and_instruments: Characterized by a lento tempo and a 2-beat bar (sometimes 4), traditional morna relies on a harmonic structure based on a cycle of fifths and is almost always monotonic. The melody features frequent syncopation, extending notes from the end of a bar to the strong beat of the next. The primary instrument is the guitar (*violão*), utilizing a specific fingerpicking and strumming technique called *mãozada* that articulates a thumb-driven bass line with arpeggiated or rhythmic chords. Ensembles also incorporate cavaquinhos, ten or twelve-string violas, violins (*rabecas*), pianos, and various percussion instruments.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed at key life events such as weddings, christenings, and family reunions. Central themes include universal subjects like love, as well as distinctively Cape Verdean realities: departure abroad, return, saudade, love for the homeland, and the sea.
sections.notable_figures: Cesária Évora, Eugénio Tavares, B. Leza (Francisco Xavier da Cruz), Bana, Celina Pereira, Teté Alhinho, Jorge Monteiro, Manuel de Novas, Ildo Lobo.
sections.regional_variants: Boa Vista morna is the oldest variant, characterized by a quicker tempo (andante ~96 bpm), rubato style, simpler structure, and satirical or social themes. Brava morna features a slower tempo (lento ~60 bpm), strong romanticism, rhymes, and a rigid meter. São Vicente morna shares the slower tempo of Brava but incorporates enriched passing chords, wider non-rigid themes, and lacks strict rhyming.
sections.lineage: Considered by some authors to be a cross between local choros and the lundum. It served as a precursor and contemporary to the coladeira.

basic_steps: Embrace partner with one arm and hold hands with the other
Sway the body twice to one side during the first musical bar
Shift and sway the body twice to the opposite side during the second musical bar
teaching.level_notes: Beginner friendly, focusing on partner connection and synchronized swaying to a slow tempo.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Syncopated, where a note at the end of a bar is extended to the strong beat of the next; accented on the first and last half-beat
music_profile.vocal_style: Emotional, lyrical, sung in Cape Verdean Creole
music_profile.musical_form: Strophic alternating with a refrain, featuring a solo instrumental intro and a middle instrumental improvisation
music_profile.sound_description: A slow, plaintive acoustic sound led by guitar fingerpicking (*mãozada*) intertwining a steady bass with arpeggiated chords, accompanied by expressive, sorrowful vocals exploring themes of longing and departure.

movement_profile.arms_and_hands: One arm embracing the partner, while with the other arm they hold hands
movement_profile.partnering: Couples dancing closely with an arm embrace and hand hold
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Lento (slow) or andante depending on regional variant

signature_moves.name: The Two-Bar Body Swing
signature_moves.description: Swaying the body twice to one side for one musical bar, then twice to the opposite side on the next bar.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Sound of Saudade: Decoding Cape Verde's Morna
episode_brief.logline: Explore the national ballroom dance of Cape Verde, where couples sway in slow, melancholic rhythm to songs of island departure and homecoming.
beats: Introduction to the islands of Cape Verde and the UNESCO recognition of morna.
The historical roots in Boa Vista and the influence of lundum and choros.
Eugénio Tavares and the birth of romantic morna in Brava.
B. Leza and the introduction of Brazilian passing chords in São Vicente.
A masterclass in the signature two-bar partner body swing.
The voice of Cesária Évora and the global resonance of the genre.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the basic partner embrace and two-bar body sway
drills: Practice solo weight shifts to a slow 2-beat count
Pair up and establish the arm-embrace and hand-hold frame
Execute the two-bar swing to a traditional morna recording

visual_motifs: Acoustic guitar strings vibrating under a thumb-led mãozada strum
Dancers swaying in pairs under dim lighting
Archival photographs of Cesária Évora performing on international stages
episode_brief.instructor_persona: A grounded Cape Verdean dance instructor emphasizing emotional connection and rhythmic listening over rigid footwork.
episode_brief.music_cue: An acoustic guitar intro featuring a slow, syncopated cycle-of-fifths progression, followed by a plaintive vocal entry.

connections.name: coladeira
connections.note: Emerged from the musical landscape of Cape Verde alongside morna, sharing harmonic roots but featuring a faster tempo.

connections.name: lundum
connections.note: An early musical genre believed to have influenced the rhythmic origins of morna.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the upper body sway and arm movements while seated in a stable chair.
seniors.standing_version: Stand with feet hip-width apart and practice the gentle weight shifts and body sways without a partner.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Reduced range of motion, maintaining a very slow tempo.

children.game_version: A mirror-sway game where children hold hands in pairs and sway together to a slow count.
children.counts: Two sways left, two sways right per bar.

gaps: Costume details and specific clothing requirements are not described in the sources.
Detailed footwork mechanics beyond the basic partner body swing are not described in sources.
